title: Ballads and the second Mardi Gras record
summary: He discusses his ballads and the later hit Mardi Gras in New Orleans, which still sells and on which he finally holds rights.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: All right. Yeah. So for Eb you did six sides. All of them were pretty good. Did you like your ballads? All your ballads were really nice. Did you like your ballads?

Yeah, I do some of the ballads today. I do the Cry Pretty Baby. The ballads were- The Cry Pretty Baby and Misery. I don't do that much anymore. Whenever you change his band you got to get the pieces to direct them to the changes and the measurements and the balls and all.
But you did have a big record for Ron, going to Mardi Gras New Orleans the second time you did it.
Yeah, that was also Mr. Joe Osanto's doctor. I believe that was for his brother-in-law, Joe Rufino. Joe Rufino. And- Now that's still popular.
Did you see any money off of that? Well- Besides being paid at the session? Really we ain't been arguing about it because- And he still sells it every year now.

Yeah, but he had been selling it every year. From here on I should draw a roll just off it. I just received a statement this year from what they claimed they made off it all of those many years. It wasn't nothing to add up to, you know. But now I do have the rights to it, you know, from here on, you know.
Right. And after- after- well for Ron you did- well Ron you did the Cutting Out and If I Only Knew, which was a nice ballad, If I Only Knew.
You know, when you were going to come out and be by the phone. But you're always right.
